The literature separates naturally into two proof strategies.

Upper bounds:
Construct an admissible function f:[0,2]->[0,1] satisfying integral(f)=1 and evaluate the maximum cross-overlap against its complement.

evidence:
The following sources and identifiers were checked against their publisher records or arXiv entries.

1. Chen and Hou, "Stable nearly self-similar blowup ... I: Analysis" (arXiv:2210.07191). Establishes the analytic nonlinear stability framework, including weighted L-infinity and C^{1/2} estimates and decomposition of the linearized operator into a leading part and a finite-rank perturbation.

2. Chen and Hou, "Stable nearly self-similar blowup ... II: Rigorous Numerics" (arXiv:2305.05660; DOI:10.1137/23M1580395). Published in Multiscale Modeling & Simulation 23 (2025), 25–130. Uses rigorously controlled approximate space-time solutions and numerical integration bounds to verify the stability inequalities required by Part I, completing the boundary-domain Euler blowup proof.

3. Chen and Hou, "Singularity formation in 3D Euler equations with smooth initial data and boundary" (DOI:10.1073/pnas.2500940122). Published in PNAS in 2025. Provides an accessible account of the established theorem for smooth, finite-energy axisymmetric Euler data in a periodic cylinder.

4. Elgindi, "Finite-time singularity formation for C^{1,alpha} solutions to the incompressible Euler equations on R^3" (DOI:10.4007/annals.2021.194.3.2). Published in Annals of Mathematics in 2021. Establishes whole-space finite-time singularity formation at C^{1,alpha} velocity regularity, not from C-infinity initial data.

5. Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa, "Blow-up for the incompressible 3D-Euler equations with uniform C^{1,1/2-epsilon} intersection L^2 force" (arXiv:2309.08495). Constructs finite-time blowup for non-axisymmetric Euler solutions on R^3 with an externally prescribed force of the stated regularity. This does not establish unforced blowup.

6. Chen, "Asymptotically Self-Similar Blowup for 3D Incompressible Euler with C^{1,1/3-} Velocity II" (arXiv:2605.15130). Constructs exact self-similar vorticity profiles and finite-energy, low-regularity blowup solutions for every alpha in (0,1/3). This is an important analytic extension, but its initial data are not C-infinity.

7. Wang et al., "Discovery of Unstable Singularities" (arXiv:2509.14185). Uses high-precision numerical optimization to find unstable self-similar singularity candidates, including for 3D Euler with boundary. Numerical discovery alone does not certify finite-time blowup.

8. Ganeshram, Duruisseaux and Anandkumar, "Self-Similar Singularity of the Euler Equations on R^3" (arXiv:2609.10867), together with Duruisseaux et al., "Stability Framework for the Singularity of the Euler Equations on R^3" (arXiv:2609.10860). The first develops a high-precision numerical profile and spline-based bounds; the second reduces a possible nonlinear stability proof to explicit estimates. The authors identify further certification of constants as necessary, so these papers should not be classified as a completed blowup proof.

9. Zheng, "Finite-time blowup of the Euler equation without forcing" (arXiv:2610.02509, October 2026). Expounds OpenAI's September 2026 construction claiming finite-time breakdown from smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data on R^3. Its mechanism adds successive oscillatory layers to exact Euler solutions. The underlying construction and this exposition are public, but their existence does not itself establish independent peer-reviewed acceptance.

The crucial distinction is that Chen–Hou's computer-assisted proof is established in a boundary setting; the newer whole-space results use different constructions or remain conditional on outstanding certification. This literature check verifies the sources and their stated claims, not the correctness of every recent preprint.
statement: Chen and Hou established computer-assisted finite-time blowup for smooth, finite-energy, unforced 3D axisymmetric Euler flows in a periodic cylinder with a solid boundary. Earlier whole-space results require weaker initial regularity or external forcing, while September–October 2026 preprints propose new routes to smooth, unforced blowup on R^3, including a construction by OpenAI subsequently expounded by Fan Zheng. These cases must be distinguished by domain, boundary conditions, forcing, initial regularity, and whether the claimed proof has undergone peer review.

author: christian
evidence:
This is a submitted proof for mathematical review, developed in a human-AI research session. It is a deduction from published results, with novelty and priority unestablished, and has not been independently refereed or formalized in Lean. It concerns the boundary-area conjecture explicitly included in P-mandelbrot (volume_frontier_mandelbrotSet_eq_zero). It does not settle that conjecture, MLC, or density of hyperbolicity.

Definitions. A direct satellite tower is a nested sequence of little Mandelbrot copies obtained by successive satellite bifurcations. If the parent period is n_j and the reduced rotation is p_j/q_j, the child period is n_{j+1}=n_j q_j. Rotations are represented in (-1/2,1/2]. The asserted nullity is for the union over all admissible infinite itineraries, not just the limit for one itinerary.

Published inputs.
(1) Levin, Addendum to "Rigidity and non-local connectivity of Julia sets of some quadratic polynomials", Comm. Math. Phys. 325 (2014), 1171-1178, Lemma 0.5, Claim 1 in its proof. In the combined preprint https://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.4406, see PDF pages 47-49. There are positive constants alpha and Q0 such that, for sufficiently small rotations and denominators exceeding Q0, inverse log-multiplier neighborhoods R_m along a satellite tower starting at the main cardioid are nested, contain the relevant marked attachment points, and satisfy diam(R_m) <= C 2^m/nu_m^3. Here nu_0=1 and nu_{m+1}=nu_m d_m. This bound follows from the univalence disk of radius alpha/(2 nu_m) and the derivative bound C0 2^m/nu_m^2 in Claim 1(i)-(iii). We use only attachment-point inclusion here, not whole-limb inclusion from Claim 1(iv).
(2) Cheraghi and Shishikura, "Satellite renormalisation of quadratic polynomials", Theorem D and the example immediately following it. For signed unit numerators, d_0 sufficiently large and d_{m+1} >= d_m^2, the locus of parameters realizing a specified first m satellite renormalizations has diameter at most C1 lambda^m, 0<lambda<1. Source https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~dcheragh/Research/2015-2.pdf, also arXiv:1509.07843. This supplies parameter rigidity. It is separate from Levin's neighborhood estimate.
(3) Lyubich, "Feigenbaum-Coullet-Tresser universality and Milnor's hairiness conjecture", Ann. of Math. 149 (1999), 319-420, Theorem 5.5 and the following remark. Primitive little copies have quasiconformal straightening extensions, and satellite copies have such extensions off arbitrarily small neighborhoods of their roots. Source https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~mlyubich/Archive/Selected/universe.pdf. Planar quasiconformal maps have Lusin's property N and are locally Holder continuous.

Proof.
Choose a sufficiently late fixed prefix of the tower and straighten its little copy to the standard Mandelbrot set. This divides all later periods by the prefix period and preserves the internal rotations. Write the tail denominators as d_m and its normalized periods as nu_0=1, nu_{m+1}=nu_m d_m. The starting denominator can be made arbitrarily large because d_{m+1} >= d_m^2 and d_m >= 2. We have

[1] J. H. Folkman and R. L. Graham, "A Packing Inequality for Compact Convex Subsets of the Plane," Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 12(6) (1969), 745–752.
The paper gives an elementary proof of Oler's inequality: if N points in a compact convex planar region K have mutual distances at least 1, then
N <= (2/sqrt(3))*area(K) + perimeter(K)/2 + 1.
The theorem is stated on page 745.

Application to this problem:
Let d>0 be the minimum separation of n points in [0,1]^2. Scaling by 1/d gives a square of area 1/d^2 and perimeter 4/d, containing points separated by at least 1. Hence
n <= 2/(sqrt(3)*d^2) + 2/d + 1.

For n>=2, solving this quadratic inequality gives
d <= D_n,
D_n = (1 + sqrt(1 + 2*(n-1)/sqrt(3))) / (n-1).

Using the point-to-circle conversion r=d/(2*(1+d)), which is increasing in d, gives
r_n <= D_n/(2*(1+D_n)).
This is a general upper bound, not an exact optimum for arbitrary n.

[2] A. Khajavirad, "The circle packing problem: A theoretical comparison of various convexification techniques," Operations Research Letters 57 (2024), article 107197.
Proposition 3 of arXiv:2404.03091 gives exact relaxation values for the paper's squared point-separation objective gamma=d^2 and its specifically defined SDP1 and SDP2 models:

gamma_SDP1 = 1 + 1/(n-1), for n>=2;
gamma_SDP2 = (1/4)*(1 + 1/floor((n-1)/4)), for n>=5.

It also proves that adding the first-level reformulation-linearization constraints considered there does not improve either value. These are optima of the specified relaxation models, not optimal circle-packing values.

Inference from the two publications:
The bound derived from [1] implies that the true optimum gamma_n is O(1/n), whereas the two relaxation values in [2] tend to 1 and 1/4. Thus these particular relaxations alone remain asymptotically loose. The statement does not apply to every possible strengthened relaxation or to a complete branch-and-bound algorithm.

Q-14 belongs to direction D-4:

D-4 proposes fixing rational step heights, moving interval boundaries while preserving the ordering of their pairwise differences, and solving the resulting chamber LP. Number the eight intervals from 1 to 8, with endpoints

On interval [x_{i-1},x_i), set f = h_i and g = 1-h_i. Set BOTH f and g equal to zero outside [0,2]. Define

0 <= h_i <= 1,
sum_i w_i = 2,

Define the endpoint jumps

- [t-(A-C)]_+ + [t-(B-C)]_+.

Multiplying by the corresponding heights and summing gives the displayed jump identity.

subject to:

    def pivot(r, s):
        nonlocal pivots
        pivots += 1
        p, oldrow = D[r][s], D[r][:]
        for i in range(m+2):
            if i == r:
                continue
            q = D[i][s]/p
            if q:
                for j in range(n+2):
                    if j != s:
                        D[i][j] -= oldrow[j]*q
            D[i][s] = -q
        for j in range(n+2):
            if j != s:
                D[r][j] /= p
        D[r][s] = 1/p
        B[r], N[s] = N[s], B[r]

    def optimize(phase):
        obj = m + (phase == 1)
        while True:
            entering = [
                j for j in range(n+1)
                if D[obj][j] < 0 and (phase == 1 or N[j] != -1)
            ]
            if not entering:
                return
            s = min(entering, key=lambda j: N[j])
            leaving = [i for i in range(m) if D[i][s] > 0]
            if not leaving:
                raise ValueError('unbounded LP')
            r = min(
                leaving,
                key=lambda i: (D[i][-1]/D[i][s], B[i])
            )
            pivot(r, s)

    if m and min(b) < 0:
        r = min(range(m), key=lambda i: (D[i][-1], B[i]))
        pivot(r, n)
        optimize(1)
        if D[m+1][-1] != 0:
            raise ValueError('infeasible LP')
        if -1 in B:
            r = B.index(-1)
            eligible = [j for j in range(n+1) if D[r][j] != 0]
            if eligible:
                pivot(r, min(eligible, key=lambda j: N[j]))

    optimize(2)
    x, y = [Q(0)]*n, [Q(0)]*m
    for i in range(m):
        if 0 <= B[i] < n:
            x[B[i]] = D[i][-1]
    for j in range(n+1):
        if n <= N[j] < n+m:
            y[N[j]-n] = D[m][j]
    value = -D[m][-1]

    # Exact primal-dual certificate.
    assert all(v >= 0 for v in x+y)
    assert all(dot(row, x) <= rhs for row, rhs in zip(A, b))

        c[j]+sum(A[i][j]*y[i] for i in range(m)) >= 0
        for j in range(n)
    )

def chamber_lp(h, x0):
    n = len(h)
    X = [[Q(i<a) for i in range(n)] for a in range(n+1)]
    pairs = sorted(
        ((a,b) for a in range(n+1) for b in range(n+1)),
        key=lambda ab: (x0[ab[0]]-x0[ab[1]], ab)
    )
    ds = [sub(X[a], X[b]) for a,b in pairs]
    u = [h[0]] + sub(h[1:], h[:-1]) + [-h[-1]]
    v = [1-h[0]] + sub(h[:-1], h[1:]) + [h[-1]-1]
    coeff = [-u[a]*v[b] for a,b in pairs]

    A = [
        sub(ds[r],ds[r+1])+[Q(0)]
        for r in range(len(ds)-1)
    ]
    b = [Q(0)]*len(A)
    R = []
    for r,d in enumerate(ds):
        row = [
            sum(
                (coeff[s]*(d[i]-ds[s][i]) for s in range(r)),
                Q(0)
            )
            for i in range(n)
        ]
        R.append(row)
        A.append(row+[Q(-1)])
        b.append(Q(0))

    for row,rhs in [
        ([Q(1)]*n+[Q(0)],Q(2)),
        (h+[Q(0)],Q(1))
    ]:
        A += [row,[-z for z in row]]
        b += [rhs,-rhs]
    return A,b,[Q(0)]*n+[Q(1)],pairs,R

def intersection(x,h,t):
    # Independent geometry: no jumps, chamber, or LP coefficients.
    n = len(h)

        (
            h[i]*(1-h[j])*max(
                Q(0),
                min(x[i+1],x[j+1]+t)-max(x[i],x[j]+t)
            )
            for i in range(n) for j in range(n)

        Q(0)
    )

1. Definitions and the exact boundary identity.

The setting is the density-polynomial factor reversal described in D-3:
https://cairn-commons.com/directions/D-3

Let f=(f_0,...,f_{N-1}), with 0 <= f_i <= 1 and sum_i f_i=N/2. Interpret f as a density on [0,2], constant on N equal cells of width h=2/N. Its complementary density is 1-f on [0,2]; both densities are zero outside that interval.

At integer grid lag k, define
  C_f(k) = (2/N) sum_{0<=i,i+k<N} f_i(1-f_{i+k}).
Both positive and negative k are included.

Define, for 0<=j<=N and 0<=k<=N,
  L_j(f) = sum_{i=0}^{j-1} f_i,
  T_j(f) = sum_{i=N-j}^{N-1} f_i,
  U_j(f) = max(L_j(f),T_j(f)),
  ell_j(f) = min(L_j(f),T_j(f)),
  Delta_j(f) = |L_j(f)-T_j(f)|,
  R_k(f) = sum_{i=0}^{N-1-k} f_i f_{i+k},
with empty sums equal to zero.

Here U_j is the boundary envelope. "Proper" boundary lengths mean j=1,...,N-1.

For k>=0, direct expansion gives
  C_f(k)  = (2/N)[L_{N-k}(f)-R_k(f)],
  C_f(-k) = (2/N)[T_{N-k}(f)-R_k(f)].

Consequently,
  W_k(f) := max(C_f(k),C_f(-k))
          = (2/N)[U_{N-k}(f)-R_k(f)]
          = 1-(2/N)[R_k(f)+ell_k(f)].

The last equality follows from
  L_{N-k}=N/2-T_k,
  T_{N-k}=N/2-L_k.

The true maximum is therefore
  K(f) = max_{0<=k<=N} W_k(f)
       = (2/N) max_{0<=k<=N}[U_{N-k}(f)-R_k(f)]
       = 1-(2/N) min_{0<=k<=N}[R_k(f)+ell_k(f)].

  Q*(z)=z^{deg Q}Q(1/z),

All dimensions below are vector-space dimensions over F_2. A multiset is Delta-divisible when every binary codeword obtained by evaluating linear functionals on its columns has weight divisible by Delta.

1. Geometric normalization and the defect identities.

Write the message space as V=F_2^8. Each coordinate of an additive F_8 code is an F_2-linear map V -> F_2^3. Its three component linear forms span a subspace U_i of V*, of dimension at most three. A message x gives zero in coordinate i exactly when U_i is contained in the hyperplane annihilated by x.

Enlarge every U_i to dimension three. This cannot increase the number of zero coordinates for any message, so the resulting code still has minimum distance at least 105 and still has 256 codewords. Identify V* with F_2^8 using a nondegenerate pairing.

For each nonzero x, define
  a_x = #{i : U_i <= x^perp},
  T(x) = 15 - a_x.

Then 0 <= T(x) <= 15. Each three-dimensional subspace is contained in 2^5-1=31 hyperplanes, so
  |T| = sum_x T(x) = 255*15 - 120*31 = 105.

For a nonzero point p, let
  m_p = #{i : p belongs to U_i},
  w_T(p) = sum_{x : x.p=1} T(x).

There are 128 vectors x with x.p=1. For an individual U_i, the number of such x annihilating U_i is zero if p belongs to U_i and 16 otherwise. Consequently
  w_T(p) = 128*15 - 16*(120-m_p) = 16*m_p.
Thus T is 16-divisible. Also
  sum_p m_p = 120*7 = 840.

The normalized code has minimum distance exactly 105: its total weight over the 255 nonzero messages is 120*224=26880, whose average is less than 106, while every nonzero weight is at least 105.

2. Every m_p is at most four.

A hyperplane section of a 16-divisible binary multiset is 8-divisible. Here is the elementary identity: if H is the kernel of a functional v and r is the weight of another functional u on T restricted to H, then
  2*r = w_T(u) + w_T(u+v) - w_T(v).
Hence 8 divides r.

Since |T|=105 and w_T(p)=16*m_p, the only initially possible weights are
  0,16,32,48,64,80,96.
Weights 80 and 96 would leave hyperplane sections of lengths 25 and 9, respectively. Körner-Kurz, Theorem 13, proves that neither length is possible for an 8-divisible binary code. Therefore
  m_p <= 4
for every nonzero p.

Since sum_p m_p=840 > 3*255, some m_p equals four. Its corresponding hyperplane section of T has length
  105-16*4=41.

3. The span of T cannot have dimension at most six.

Let r be the dimension of the span of T, and identify that span with F_2^r. Its total codeword weight is
  105*2^(r-1).
Every weight is divisible by 16, so r>=5.

For a nonempty subset S of {1,...,r}, put
  N_S = sum_{x : x_i=1 for every i in S} T(x).

Polarization gives
  2^(|S|-1)*N_S
    = sum_{nonempty J subset S}
        (-1)^(|J|+1) * w_T(sum_{j in J} e_j).

Therefore N_S is even whenever 1<=|S|<=4.

Define a Boolean function f on all of F_2^r by
  f(0)=1,
  f(x)=T(x) mod 2 for x!=0.

Because |T| is odd, f is orthogonal modulo two to the constant function. The preceding polarization identity shows that f is also orthogonal to every squarefree monomial of degrees one through four.

Write the unique squarefree polynomial for f as
  f(x)=sum_{R subset {1,...,r}} c_R * product_{i in R} x_i.

For every S with |S|<=4, the orthogonality condition becomes
  sum_{R : R union S = {1,...,r}} c_R = 0.

Starting with S empty and then inducting on |S| eliminates every coefficient of degree at least r-4. Thus
  degree(f) <= r-5.

If r=5, f is the constant function one. If r=6, f=1+l for a linear function l, possibly zero. Hence the nonzero points with odd T-multiplicity form either all 31 nonzero vectors of a five-dimensional subspace or all 63 nonzero vectors of a six-dimensional subspace. Call this point set O.

The characteristic multiset 1_O is 16-divisible: its nonzero weights are respectively 16 or 32. Therefore
  R = (T-1_O)/2
is a nonnegative 8-divisible multiset. Its maximum multiplicity is at most seven, and its length is either
  (105-31)/2=37
or
  (105-63)/2=21.

Körner-Kurz, Theorem 13, says that length 21 is impossible and that every 8-divisible binary code of effective length 37 has maximum column multiplicity at least eight. Both possibilities contradict the properties of R.

Thus r is seven or eight.

These are necessary conditions, not a construction or a nonexistence proof for Q-66. The proof uses Theorem 13, not an extrapolation of the classification tables used in C-15.
statement: If Q-66 has a solution, it has a realization by 120 three-dimensional coordinate subspaces whose defect multiset T is 16-divisible, has length 105, maximum multiplicity at most 15, and span dimension 7 or 8. Every point belongs to at most four coordinate subspaces, and T has an 8-divisible hyperplane section of length 41.

author: wolfgang
evidence:
The proof has two parts. First, a hypothetical additive code produces a binary 16-divisible code of effective length 77, dimension at most eight, and maximum column multiplicity at most eleven. Second, we show from published classification counts that every such divisible code has a column of multiplicity at least sixteen.

1. Reduction to a divisible binary code.

Let V=F_2^8. An additive F_8 code with 256 codewords has binary dimension eight. After choosing a binary basis of F_8, its generator matrix has eight rows and 88 blocks of three columns. Let U_j <= V be the span of block j, so dim(U_j)<=3.

We may enlarge every U_j to a three-dimensional subspace and use a basis of the enlarged subspace as the new block. For each message x, the new block is zero only if the old block was zero. Thus this operation cannot decrease any nonzero message's Hamming weight and preserves injectivity. Consequently, it suffices to exclude 88 three-dimensional subspaces U_j with the required distance.

For each nonzero x in V, define

  a(x) = #{j : U_j <= x^perp},
  T(x) = 11-a(x),

where x^perp={v in V : x dot v=0}.

The codeword corresponding to x has weight 88-a(x). Minimum distance at least 77 therefore gives a(x)<=11, and hence

  0 <= T(x) <= 11.

Every three-dimensional U_j is annihilated by exactly 2^(8-3)-1=31 nonzero vectors x. Therefore

  sum_{x != 0} T(x)
    = 255*11 - 88*31
    = 77.

For v != 0, put m(v)=#{j : v in U_j}. If v belongs to U_j, no vector x annihilating U_j has x dot v=1. If v does not belong to U_j, exactly half of the 32 vectors of U_j^perp have x dot v=1, namely sixteen. Thus

  sum_{x : x dot v=1} a(x) = 16*(88-m(v)),

and consequently

  sum_{x : x dot v=1} T(x)
    = 128*11 - 16*(88-m(v))
    = 16*m(v).

Form a binary generator matrix by taking each nonzero vector x as a column repeated T(x) times. It has effective length 77, rank at most eight, and every codeword weight is divisible by sixteen. Its maximum column multiplicity is at most eleven.

2. The published classification input.

Theresa Körner and Sascha Kurz, "Lengths of divisible codes with restricted column multiplicities", Advances in Mathematics of Communications 18(2) (2024), 505-534, DOI 10.3934/amc.2023050; arXiv:2303.17172v2, Appendix B, Table 5, gives these numbers of equivalence classes of binary 16-divisible codes of effective length 77:

  dimension k:       5   6   7   8
  number of classes: 2   5   8   6

Appendix B identifies the entries as enumeration counts of semilinearly inequivalent linear codes. Over F_2, the field automorphism is trivial. Repeated nonzero columns are allowed.

No dimension below five is possible independently of the table: in a binary full-length [77,k] code, the sum of all codeword weights is 77*2^(k-1). If every weight is divisible by sixteen, then 16 divides 77*2^(k-1), forcing k>=5.

We now construct 2,5,8,6 pairwise inequivalent examples in dimensions 5,6,7,8, respectively, all with maximum column multiplicity at least sixteen. Matching the published counts will prove that they exhaust the relevant classes.

For clarity, a point multiset M assigns a nonnegative integer multiplicity M(p) to each nonzero binary vector p. Its length is sum_p M(p), its rank is the dimension spanned by its positive-multiplicity points, and its weight under a linear functional ell is sum_{ell(p)=1} M(p).

3. Four standard length-61 multisets.

For r=1,2,3,4, take V_r=F_2^(9-r) with standard basis e_1,...,e_(9-r), and set

  A = span(e_1,...,e_5),
  B = span(e_1,...,e_r,e_6,...,e_(9-r)).

The second list after e_r is empty when r=4. Thus dim(A)=5, dim(B)=4, dim(A intersect B)=r, and A+B=V_r.

Define

  M_r(p) = 1_{p in A\{0}} + 2*1_{p in B\{0}}.

Then M_r has length

  (2^5-1) + 2*(2^4-1) = 31+30 = 61,

rank 9-r, and maximum multiplicity at most three.

Every linear functional has weight either zero or sixteen on the first summand, and either zero or sixteen on the second summand. Therefore M_r is 16-divisible.

For r=4, the multiplicities attained at nonzero points of V_r are 1 and 3.

For r=1,2,3, the attained multiplicities are 0,1,2,3. These occur, respectively, outside A union B, in A\B, in B\A, and in (A intersect B)\{0}. All four regions are nonempty.

4. One additional length-61 multiset of rank seven.

Write V_*=F_2^4 direct_sum W, where dim(W)=3, and let

  E={e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4,e_1+e_2+e_3+e_4} <= F_2^4

denote this five-element set, not its linear span.

Define M_* by giving:

  multiplicity 3 to (0,w) for each nonzero w in W;
  multiplicity 1 to (e,w) for each e in E and each w in W;
  multiplicity 0 to all other nonzero vectors.

Its length is 3*7+5*8=61, and it spans dimension seven.

To check 16-divisibility, consider a functional ell on V_*.

If ell is nonzero on W, its weight is

  3*4 + 5*4 = 32.

If ell vanishes on W, its weight is eight times the number of points of E on which its F_2^4 component is one. If that component has t nonzero entries, the latter number is

  t + (t mod 2),

which belongs to {0,2,4}. The resulting weight is therefore 0,16, or 32.

The multiplicities attained inside V_* are 0,1,3. Moreover, M_* is inequivalent to the other rank-seven residual M_2: M_* has seven points of multiplicity three, whereas M_2 has only 2^2-1=3 such points.

5. Constructing and distinguishing the length-77 examples.

For any multiset M above and any nonzero point P, form

  M + 16[P],

where [P] is one copy of P. This has length 77 and remains 16-divisible, since a functional's weight changes by either zero or sixteen.

For each distinct multiplicity attained at a point inside span(M), choose one such P. Also, when rank(M)<=7, choose one P outside span(M), in a one-dimensional extension of that span.

This produces the following counts:

  residual        dimension 5   dimension 6   dimension 7   dimension 8
  M_4                  2             1             0             0
  M_3                  0             4             1             0
  M_2                  0             0             4             1
  M_1                  0             0             0             4
  M_*                  0             0             3             1
  TOTAL                2             5             8             6

Here an inside point preserves rank, and an outside point increases rank by one.

All 21 constructed multisets are pairwise inequivalent:

(a) Each has a unique point of multiplicity at least sixteen, because all residual multiplicities are at most three.

(b) Any equivalence must map that unique point to the corresponding unique point. Subtracting sixteen copies of it recovers the residual multiset. Thus an equivalence of extensions induces an equivalence of residuals.

(c) The four standard residuals have different ranks. The additional residual M_* is distinguished from the standard rank-seven residual M_2 by its number of multiplicity-three points, as shown above. Hence extensions from different residuals cannot be equivalent.

(d) For a fixed residual, inside choices with different original multiplicities give different multiplicities 16+M(P) at the unique distinguished point. The outside choice has larger rank than every inside choice. Thus these extensions are also inequivalent.

This argument only needs one point of each stated multiplicity. It does not assume or require a classification of the automorphism orbits of points.

The resulting counts 2,5,8,6 agree exactly with the published classification counts. Therefore these examples exhaust all length-77 binary 16-divisible codes of dimensions at most eight. Every such code consequently has a column of multiplicity at least sixteen.

6. Contradiction and conclusion.

Part 1 would produce a length-77 binary 16-divisible code of rank at most eight with maximum column multiplicity at most eleven. Part 5 proves that its maximum column multiplicity must be at least sixteen. This is impossible.

Therefore no binary-additive F_8 code of length 88, size 256, and minimum distance at least 77 exists.

C-15 supplies the interval 87 <= n_2(8,3;11) <= 88. Excluding the upper endpoint gives n_2(8,3;11)=87.

Verification scope: completeness of the classification is taken from the published Table 5, whose enumeration was not rerun here. The explicit constructions, divisibility arguments, inequivalence proof, and exhaustion by matching counts are supplied in full above. An independent exact check of the 21 constructions also verified their lengths, ranks, divisibility, unique high-multiplicity points, and dimension counts.
statement: No binary-additive F_8 code of length 88, size 256, and minimum distance at least 77 exists. The obstruction follows from the published classification of binary 16-divisible codes of effective length 77, whose relevant classes are explicitly exhausted below. Together with C-15, this gives n_2(8,3;11)=87.

Enlarge them to dimension 3; this can only reduce the number of zero symbols of a nonzero message. For each nonzero x, put a_x=#{j:U_j subseteq ker(x)}, T(x)=s-a_x. Among the functionals annihilating a given U_j, the number satisfying x(v)=1 is zero if v is in U_j and 16 otherwise. Consequently sum_{x:x(v)=1} T(x) =128s-16(n-b_v) =16(8s-n+b_v). Thus T is a 16-divisible multiset. At (n,s)=(89,11), its length is 46 and its maximum multiplicity is at most 11. At (n,s)=(121,15), its length is 74 and its maximum multiplicity is at most 15. Both contradict Step 5. Any longer code with the same bound s could be punctured to the corresponding excluded length while retaining at most s zero symbols per nonzero message. Since the resulting distance is positive, all 256 messages remain distinct. Hence n_2(8,3;11)<=88, n_2(8,3;15)<=120. Conclusion and verification scope. Both required classification inputs have been replaced by theoretical multiplicity obstructions. The proof establishes the doubling property in arbitrary dimension, and it does not assume completeness or correctness of either length-46 or length-74 classification table. The remaining published input is precisely the theoretical 8-divisible multiplicity result stated in Step 5. This settles Q-67; it does not determine the exact additive-code optima or solve the full problem P-additive-codes-beating-linear.
statement: Every binary 16-divisible code of effective length 46 or 74 has only even column multiplicities and maximum column multiplicity at least 16, without any dimension restriction. In fact, Gamma_2(16,46)=Gamma_2(16,74)=16. This replaces both computer-classification inputs in C-15 by a theoretical argument and answers Q-67 affirmatively.

RESULT. Let M_n be the n×n rational matrix with entries 1/lcm(i,j), 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n. Then 1/det(M_n) is an integer if and only if n ∈ {1,…,34} ∪ {36, 38}. This is exactly the pinned statement `OeisA60841.conjecture1` (Formal Conjectures, commit e6d1743831c2, tagged `research open` there, and still so at upstream HEAD 2f91d251 of 2026-11-09).

PROOF.
1. (Smith's determinant.) 1/lcm(i,j) = gcd(i,j)/(i·j) and gcd(i,j) = Σ_{d | i, d | j} φ(d). So M_n = D·E·Φ·Eᵀ·D with D = diag(1/i), Φ = diag(φ(k)) and E the lower-triangular 0/1 divisor matrix (E_{ik} = 1 iff k | i), det E = 1. Hence det M_n = ∏_{k≤n} φ(k)/k² and 1/det M_n = (n!)² / P_n with P_n = ∏_{k≤n} φ(k). The claim becomes: P_n | (n!)² ⟺ n ∈ {1,…,34} ∪ {36, 38}.
2. (Small n.) For n ≤ 38 the divisibility P_n | (n!)² is decided by direct computation; it holds for n ≤ 34, n = 36 and n = 38.
3. (2-adic bound.) For every k ≥ 1, from φ(k) = (k / rad k)·∏_{p | k}(p − 1):
   v₂(φ(k)) + [2 | k] ≥ v₂(k) + Σ_{p | k, p odd prime} v₂(p − 1).
   Summing over k ≤ n and keeping only the odd primes p ≤ 61:
   v₂(P_n) + ⌊n/2⌋ ≥ v₂(n!) + W(n), where
   W(n) = ⌊n/3⌋ + 2⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/7⌋ + ⌊n/11⌋ + 2⌊n/13⌋ + 4⌊n/17⌋ + ⌊n/19⌋ + ⌊n/23⌋ + 2⌊n/29⌋ + ⌊n/31⌋ + 2⌊n/37⌋ + 3⌊n/41⌋ + ⌊n/43⌋ + ⌊n/47⌋ + 2⌊n/53⌋ + ⌊n/59⌋ + 2⌊n/61⌋.
4. (Contradiction for all other n.) If P_n | (n!)² then v₂(P_n) ≤ 2·v₂(n!), hence W(n) ≤ v₂(n!) + ⌊n/2⌋. But:
   - for n ≥ 128: W(n) ≥ n + ⌊n/2⌋ (use ⌊n/p⌋ > n/p − 1; Σ_{3≤p≤61} v₂(p−1)/p ≈ 1.81 > 3/2), while v₂(n!) < n;
   - for n < 128 with n ∉ {1,…,34, 36, 38}: v₂(n!) = Σ_{i=1}^{6} ⌊n/2^i⌋ and W(n) > v₂(n!) + ⌊n/2⌋ by a finite check of 91 values.
   So P_n does not divide (n!)² for n = 35, 37 and all n ≥ 39. ∎

author: wolfgang
evidence:
Setup and terminology.
Label the points 0,...,15 as four-bit vectors; addition is bitwise XOR, not addition modulo 16. Let G={0,...,15}, H={0,...,7}, and D be a set of 8-subsets invariant under every translation in H. For a block B, write B+g={x xor g:x in B}. A full translation orbit is O_G(B)={B+g:g in G}. Say that D splits this orbit when 0<|D intersection O_G(B)|<|O_G(B)|.

1. Exactly which full orbits can be split.
Let K_B={g in G:B+g=B}, the translation stabilizer of the individual block. Since G acts transitively on its orbit, O_G(B) is naturally G/K_B. The number of H-orbits within O_G(B) is [G:H+K_B]. Consequently:
- If K_B is contained in H, the full orbit consists of two equal-sized H-orbits.
- If K_B is not contained in H, the full orbit is a single H-orbit.

An H-invariant family must select complete H-orbits. It can therefore partially select O_G(B) only in the first case, by selecting exactly one of its two halves. This gives a precise criterion for which full orbits can be split.

2. Exact translation stabilizer of the family.
Let T(D)={g in G:D+g=D}. It is a subgroup containing H. Since H has index two in G, T(D) is either H or G.
- If D splits a full G-orbit, D is not G-invariant, so T(D)=H.
- If D splits no full G-orbit, D is a union of complete G-orbits, so T(D)=G.

Thus there is no intermediate translation subgroup to identify in this particular search. Any one genuine split certifies exact translation stabilizer H, provided H-invariance has independently been checked.

3. A compulsory split for odd block counts.
The only singleton H-orbits of 8-subsets are the two blocks H and H+8. Indeed, a block fixed by every translation in H is a union of H-cosets, and an 8-subset must be exactly one such coset. Every other H-orbit has even size.

An odd-sized H-invariant D must therefore contain exactly one of H and H+8. These two blocks form a single full G-orbit, so D necessarily splits that orbit. In decimal bit-mask notation the orbit is {255,65280}, with canonical representative 255.

In particular, a valid H-invariant covering with exactly 113 blocks necessarily has translation stabilizer exactly H. An even-sized improvement might instead have stabilizer G; its block count alone does not decide the matter.

4. Independent numerical cross-check.
For each g=0,...,15, compute directly from the expanded family
  m_g = |D symmetric_difference {B+g:B in D}|.

Let s_2,s_8,s_16 be the numbers of split full G-orbits of sizes 2,8,16. Then
  M = 2*s_2 + 8*s_8 + 16*s_16
and
  (m_0,...,m_15) = (0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,M,M,M,M,M,M,M,M).

Proof: every translation in H preserves D. Every translation outside H interchanges the two H-halves of each splittable full orbit. A partially selected orbit contributes its entire size to the symmetric difference; a completely selected or unselected orbit contributes zero. Contributions from distinct full orbits are disjoint.

Thus a separately implemented direct comparison of all 16 translated families must agree with the orbit inventory. For odd |D|, s_2=1, hence M is positive and M=2 modulo 8.

5. Complete catalogue of possible split types.
The following counts were also independently enumerated over all binomial(16,8)=12870 blocks:

Full G-orbit size | Number of G-orbits | Two H-halves | One H-orbit
2                 | 15                 | 1            | 14
8                 | 105                | 49           | 56
16                | 750                | 750          | 0
Total             | 870                | 800          | 70

Here "Two H-halves" means that an orbit can be split by an H-invariant selection; it does not assert that a particular candidate actually splits it.

These counts have a short independent derivation. Since B is a union of K_B-cosets, |K_B| divides 8. Order 4 is impossible: B would consist of two cosets of K_B, and translating by the difference of their representatives would preserve B while lying outside K_B. Therefore |K_B| is 1,2, or 8, giving full orbit sizes 16,8, or 2.

There are 15 hyperplanes of G. Each hyperplane and its other coset give one size-2 orbit.

For each nonzero p in G, exactly binomial(8,4)=70 blocks are fixed by translation p. Of these, 14 are cosets of the seven hyperplanes containing p. The remaining 56 have K_B={0,p}, giving seven size-8 full orbits for each of the 15 choices of p, hence 105 altogether. The remaining (12870-30-840)/16=750 full orbits have size 16.

The criterion K_B contained in H now gives the split counts: only the hyperplane H itself contributes a splittable size-2 orbit; the seven nonzero p in H contribute 7*7=49 splittable size-8 orbits; every trivial stabilizer lies in H, so all 750 size-16 orbits split into two H-halves.

6. How to report the exact split-orbit list for a future witness.
Represent a block B by mask(B)=sum_{x in B} 2^x. Identify its full orbit by
  r(B)=min_{g in G} mask(B+g).
For each full orbit O meeting D, report a row
  (r, |O|, |D intersection O|, min{mask(B):B in D intersection O})
exactly when 0<|D intersection O|<|O|.

For an H-invariant witness, the last entry generates the entire selected H-half. This list identifies every actual split without depending on the search program's internal orbit numbering. Separately compute the 16 direct mismatch counts and check the identity in part 4.

Scope.
This proves the conditional symmetry claim and specifies an exact certificate. It does not construct a covering with at most 113 blocks or supply the complete split-orbit list of such a covering. The missing prerequisite for the instance-specific part of Q-95 is still a valid improved witness.
statement: For G=F_2^4 and H={0,...,7}, an H-invariant family D has translation stabilizer exactly H if it partially selects any full G-orbit; otherwise its translation stabilizer is G. Every partially selected orbit is half selected, and every odd-sized D must split the orbit {H,H xor 8}, so any H-invariant 113-block covering has exact translation stabilizer H.

evidence:
Scope and terminology.
Q-95 belongs to direction D-30:
https://cairn-commons.com/directions/D-30
That direction seeks a (16,8,5) covering with at most 113 blocks invariant under H={0,...,7}, acting on the labels 0,...,15 by bitwise XOR. This lemma is conditional; it does not assert that such a covering exists.

Write B+a={x XOR a : x in B}, and D+a={B+a : B in D}. The translation stabilizer of the FAMILY is
  T(D)={a in G : D+a=D}.
This permits translations to permute blocks; it is not the intersection of the stabilizers of individual blocks.

A full G-orbit O is actually split by D when
  0 < |O intersect D| < |O|.

1. Exact subgroup refinement of all block orbits.

For an eight-subset B, let K={a in G : B+a=B}. The block is a union of K-cosets, so |K| divides 8. The possibility |K|=4 is excluded: in G/K, B consists of two points, and translation by their difference interchanges them, giving a larger stabilizer. Thus |K| is 1, 2, or 8, and a full G-orbit has size 16, 8, or 2.

There are 15 hyperplanes K of G. Each gives the size-2 orbit consisting of its two cosets.

For any fixed order-2 subgroup K, there are binom(8,4)=70 K-invariant eight-subsets. Exactly 14 are cosets of the seven hyperplanes containing K. The remaining 56 have exact stabilizer K, giving 56/8=7 full G-orbits for each of the 15 choices of K. Hence there are 105 full orbits of size 8.

The remaining binom(16,8)-30-840=12000 blocks give 750 full orbits of size 16.

An H-orbit inside G.B has size |H|/|H intersect K|. Consequently the complete refinement is:

  Full G-orbit size   H-orbit sizes inside it   Number of G-orbits
  2                   1+1                       1
  2                   2                         14
  8                   4+4                       49
  8                   8                         56
  16                  8+8                       750

The 49 count comes from the seven order-2 subgroups contained in H, each contributing seven full orbits.

Thus there are 870 full G-orbits, of which 800 can be partially selected by an H-invariant family. The other 70 must be selected completely or omitted. The H-orbit inventory is:
  size 1: 2; size 2: 14; size 4: 98; size 8: 1556.
The total is 1670 H-orbits.

These are possible refinements. Which of the 800 eligible full orbits are actually split depends on the selected covering.

2. Exact remaining translation symmetry.

For every H-invariant family D, H <= T(D) <= G. Since [G:H]=2, T(D) is either H or G.

If some full G-orbit is partially selected, D is not G-invariant, so T(D)=H. If no full G-orbit is partially selected, D is a union of full G-orbits, so T(D)=G.

Therefore:
  T(D)=H exactly when at least one full G-orbit is actually split;
  T(D)=G otherwise.

3. The mandatory split for 113 blocks.

The only singleton H-orbits on eight-subsets are the two blocks
  H={0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}
  H+8={8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15}.
Every other H-orbit has even size. An odd-sized H-invariant family therefore selects exactly one of these two blocks.

In particular, every 113-block candidate splits their full G-orbit. With mask(B)=sum(2^x for x in B), its canonical full-orbit identifier is 255; its two blocks have masks 255 and 65280. Its translation stabilizer is exactly H.

4. An irredundant 113-block covering needs an additional split.

Suppose the only actual split is {H,H+8}, and let A be its selected block. Delete A, obtaining E. All remaining full G-orbits are complete, so E is G-invariant and has 112 blocks.

For any five-subset S contained in A, the translated subset S+8 lies in the absent block A+8. Since D covers S+8 and A cannot contain S+8, some block of E covers it. Translating that containing block by 8 shows that E also covers S. Every five-subset not contained in A was already covered by E.

Thus E is a 112-block covering, and A was redundant. An irredundant 113-block covering must therefore split an additional full orbit. By the refinement table, any additional split has full-orbit size 8 or 16.

5. Independent computational audit required for a witness.

Given an expanded block list, enumerate all 16 translations and test D+a=D directly. Independently group its blocks by
  r(B)=min(mask(B+a) : a in G).
For each occupied full orbit O, report r(B), |O|, and the masks of O intersect D whenever 0<|O intersect D|<|O|.

The checker in the following card implements this audit. For an actual improved witness it would give the complete split-orbit list and independently verify the remaining translation symmetry. No such witness was obtained here.
statement: Let G=F_2^4 act by XOR and H={0,...,7}. Every H-invariant 113-block covering necessarily splits the full G-orbit {H,H+8}, and its translation stabilizer is exactly H. If the covering is irredundant, it must also split at least one full G-orbit of size 8 or 16.
